cues.text: Let us turn now to additional examples of digital business models and the strategic role of information technology.
We begin with what a digital business model actually is.
Digital business models typically combine several features: a digital core, customer-centricity, data-driven decisions, agility, scalability, and sometimes network effects.
A digital core means that the main way the business creates and delivers value runs on digital technology, rather than technology being a side tool.
Customer-centricity means the design starts from what customers need.
Data-driven decisions means the organisation uses evidence from its own data to guide choices.
Agility is the ability to change quickly.
Scalability is the ability to grow without costs and problems growing at the same rate.
And network effects occur when a service becomes more valuable as more people use it, though the source says only "sometimes", so not every digital business has them.
That leads to an important caution: not every digital business is a platform.
A platform brings different groups together, but many digital businesses do not do this.
So we should separate business models by how they earn revenue.
Direct e-commerce earns sales revenue, because the business sells goods and is paid for each sale.
Subscriptions earn recurring access fees, meaning customers pay repeatedly for continued access.
Transaction platforms collect commissions, taking a share of the transactions that happen between the parties they connect.
Advertising-supported services monetise audience attention through advertisements, so the audience may not pay directly; advertisers pay to reach that audience.
Freemium converts some free users to paid plans, so many people use the basic service free, and a portion upgrade.
Finally, on-demand describes service timing, not necessarily how revenue is collected.
An on-demand service gives you the service when you ask for it, but the money might come from a commission, a fee, or something else.
So on-demand is about when, not how it is paid for.
Now let us look at the table of teaching examples.
It has three columns: the teaching example, the value proposition, and the enabling IT and trade-off.
I will go through each row in order.
First row, Amazon.
Its value proposition is online convenience, broad selection and marketplace access.
The enabling IT is elastic infrastructure, data and logistics.
The trade-off is that it must manage platform quality and fulfilment cost.
Second row, Netflix.
Its value proposition is on-demand subscription streaming.
Notice how this combines the two ideas we just separated: on-demand describes the timing, and subscription describes the revenue.
The enabling IT is content delivery, recommendations and data analytics.
The trade-offs are content cost and changing preferences.
Third row, Uber.
Its value proposition is to coordinate riders and drivers.
The enabling IT is GPS, mobile applications, matching and payments.
The trade-offs are safety, supply and regulatory requirements.
Fourth row, Airbnb.
Its value proposition is to connect accommodation hosts and travellers.
The enabling IT is search, reviews, trust and payments.
The trade-offs are quality assurance and local rules.
Fifth row, Paystack, a Nigerian example.
Its value proposition is to simplify payment acceptance.
The enabling IT is APIs, payment integration and reliable processing.
An API, or application programming interface, is an agreed way for one piece of software to talk to another.
The trade-offs are fraud, reconciliation and uptime.
Reconciliation means checking that records of payments match across systems, and uptime means how reliably the service stays available.
Sixth row, Kuda, also a Nigerian example.
Its value proposition is digitally delivered banking workflows.
The enabling IT is mobile services and integrated operations.
The trade-offs are trust, resilience and inclusion.
Notice the pattern in every row: each benefit comes paired with a cost or risk.
Technology enables the value, but the organisation must still manage the trade-off.
Next, the strategic role of IT.
IT has four broad strategic jobs: improve customer experience, optimise processes, enable new products and business models, and support informed decisions.
Secure and reliable delivery underpins all four, so if systems are insecure or unreliable, none of the four jobs can be done well.
Two technical terms matter here.
Scalability means handling increased demand without unacceptable degradation, so the service keeps working acceptably as more people use it.
Elasticity adjusts allocated capacity as demand changes, meaning capacity can expand when demand rises and be reduced when it falls.
And global 24/7 digital reach requires reliable service, payments, localisation and customer support.
Localisation means adapting the service to local language, currency and conditions.
Before investing, an organisation should assess maturity across these areas: infrastructure, integration, skills, customer experience, process automation, data governance, leadership and resilience.
The guidance is to prioritise gaps that prevent business outcomes rather than chasing a technology checklist.
In other words, invest where a weakness blocks results, not simply to own the latest tools.
Finally, the worked comparison.
A retailer with physical stores and online checkout has added a digital sales channel.
Now suppose inventory, pricing, fulfilment and support are still siloed, meaning separate and not connected.
Then customers may order unavailable items, because the website does not truly know what the stores or warehouse hold.
Integrating inventory and delivery can improve digitalisation, which is using digital technology to improve how existing processes work.
Redesigning the business around a unified omnichannel service and new revenue opportunities constitutes broader transformation.
Omnichannel means store, online and other channels working together as one experience.
The lesson is that adding a channel is not the same as transforming the business, and the source's closing rule is to use actual outcomes to judge the change.
What matters is not the label, but what really changes for customers and for the organisation.
